doc.title: Ruthie Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 28, 2023

title: Wayne Jackson's muted trumpet on 'I Really Love You'
summary: Wayne Jackson of the Memphis Horns came without written music and surprised everyone with a muted trumpet part.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: I liked a moment that happened on — I think it was the tune “I Really Love You” from the “Truth According to Ruthie Foster.” Wayne Jackson and this little muted trumpet thing. It just sounded so spontaneous.

Yeah. I think it was. We didn’t expect him to pick up the mute for his trumpet. Because he didn’t rehearse it that way when we were going over the song. And Wayne was one of those people where he showed up, and I didn’t realize this: these guys, the Memphis Horns is what you’re talking about, Wayne Jackson and the Memphis Horns, they didn’t show up with music at all. And I thought that was really odd coming from a girl who — you know I went to school for music and that’s what horn players do usually when they show up to a studio. And Wayne just wanted to hear the song, he wanted to have us just play it through a few times. And he said, “Um hum” and he had his horn with him right there in the control room and he’s playing a few parts. And I see him, he’s talking to the guys. And I think he was just telling them what — “You’re going to do the third here, you do the fifth and then we’ll scoot down to the” blah-blah-blah. And it went on. And we played it through a couple of more times and he went into the studio and the part came up. And I saw him pick up the mute for the horn and I’m thinking okay what’s he doing, this is different. And that’s what came out, what you’re hearing on that particular © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
song. And it’s perfect, absolutely perfect how that turned out. Genius. Loved working with Wayne.
